q: In which year was the Negotiable Instruments Act enacted in India?
explain: The Negotiable Instruments Act was enacted in 1881. The RBI Act of 1934 is a different law, though the NI Act works subject to its Sections 31 and 32.

q: Before the Negotiable Instruments Act of 1881 was enacted, which law applied in India?
explain: The English law applied earlier, and the Indian Act of 1881 is itself based on the English Act with some modifications.

q: The Negotiable Instruments Act operates subject to Sections 31 and 32 of which Act?
explain: Sections 31 and 32 of the RBI Act, 1934 limit how instruments payable to bearer can be issued, and the NI Act works subject to them.

q: Under Section 13(a), a negotiable instrument means a promissory note, a bill of exchange or a
explain: The three instruments recognised by statute are the promissory note, the bill of exchange and the cheque, payable to order or to bearer.

q: Which instrument can never be made payable to the bearer, whether on demand or after a certain time?
options: Bill of exchange payable after a certain time
explain: A promissory note cannot be made payable to the bearer. A cheque can be bearer on demand, and a bill can be bearer after a time.

q: Which statement is correct about payable-to-bearer instruments?
options: A promissory note can be made payable to bearer on demand
A bill of exchange can be made payable to bearer on demand
A cheque can never be drawn payable to bearer
A bill of exchange cannot be made payable to bearer on demand
explain: A bill cannot be bearer on demand, though it can be bearer after a certain time. A cheque, drawn on a banker, may be bearer on demand.

q: A bona fide transferee for value who is not affected by defects in the title of earlier holders is called a
explain: A holder in due course takes the instrument in good faith and for value, and gets a clean title.

q: A negotiable instrument can be transferred any number of times until it reaches
explain: Transfer by negotiation can continue as long as the instrument has not matured.

q: The transferee of a negotiable instrument can sue in his own name in case of
explain: The right to sue in his own name on dishonour is one of the rights of the transferee.

q: It is not necessary to write ‘for value received’ in a promissory note because
explain: Consideration is presumed for every negotiable instrument until the contrary is proved, so those words add nothing.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a negotiable instrument?
explain: The characteristics are property, title, rights, presumptions and prompt payment. Crossing is a feature of cheques only and is not compulsory.

q: A holder of a negotiable instrument can expect prompt payment because dishonour
options: ruins the credit of all persons who are parties to it
is a punishable offence for the holder
explain: Because dishonour would ruin the credit of every party, parties pay promptly.

q: Which sections of the Negotiable Instruments Act lay down presumptions about negotiable instruments?
explain: Sections 118 and 119 list the presumptions that the court makes without needing proof.

q: Where a negotiable instrument is dated, the court presumes that it
options: was made or drawn on that date unless the contrary is proved
must be paid on the same day
explain: The presumption as to date means the date written on the instrument is taken as its date of making unless disproved.

q: Under Section 119, on proof of protest the court presumes
explain: In a suit on a dishonoured instrument, proof of protest leads the court to presume dishonour until it is disproved.

q: Which of the following is NOT a presumption under Section 118?
options: That the instrument was made for consideration
That endorsements were made in the order in which they appear
That a transfer was made before maturity
explain: Consideration, date, time of acceptance, time of transfer, order of endorsement, stamp and holder in due course are presumed. Solvency is not.

q: A lost promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque is presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have been
explain: Stamp is one of the presumptions: a lost instrument is presumed to have been duly stamped.

q: Until the contrary is proved, the holder of a negotiable instrument is presumed to be
explain: Every holder is presumed to have paid consideration and taken the instrument in good faith, so is presumed a holder in due course.

q: Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act deals with
explain: Section 4 defines the promissory note, Section 5 the bill of exchange and Section 6 the cheque.

q: Which section of the Negotiable Instruments Act deals with the cheque?
explain: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand.

q: A bill of exchange is
explain: A bill of exchange contains an unconditional order directing a certain person to pay. A promissory note contains a promise.

q: Which of the following is correct about a promissory note?
options: It need not be in writing
The promise to pay must be definite and unconditional
The payment can be in kind
explain: A promissory note must be in writing, with a definite and unconditional undertaking to pay a certain sum of money.

q: How many parties are involved in a promissory note?
explain: A promissory note has two parties: the maker (debtor) who promises to pay and the payee (creditor) who receives.

q: Which of the following is recognised as a negotiable instrument by usage or custom rather than by statute?
explain: Promissory notes, bills and cheques are statutory. Hundis, share warrants, dividend warrants, railway receipts and the like are recognised by custom.

q: All of the following are recognised by custom rather than by statute, EXCEPT
explain: A promissory note is recognised by the statute itself. The other three are customary or quasi-negotiable instruments.

q: An instrument that is incomplete in some respects under the Negotiable Instruments Act is called a/an
explain: An inchoate instrument is one that is incomplete and can be completed later by the holder.

q: A hundi is a negotiable instrument written in
explain: A hundi is an indigenous negotiable instrument in an oriental language, whether in the form of a note or a bill.

q: A cheque is a bill of exchange with two more qualifications. Which pair is correct?
options: Drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand
Payable after a fixed time and drawn on a company
Payable only to the bearer and only in cash
explain: A cheque is always drawn on a specified banker and always payable on demand.

q: Which of the following is NOT a classification of bills of exchange?
explain: Bills are classified as inland and foreign, time and demand, and trade and accommodation bills.

q: Truncated cheques come under which Act?
explain: Truncated cheques are covered by the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

q: Which of the following Acts helps a bank in its day-to-day activities?
explain: Cheques, drafts and other instruments that banks handle daily are governed by the Negotiable Instruments Act.

q: A negotiable financial instrument issued by a bank to represent a foreign company’s publicly traded securities is a
explain: A depository receipt represents shares of a foreign company and is issued by a bank. The other options do not represent securities.

q: Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act extends protection to the
explain: Section 131 protects the collecting banker who collects a cheque in good faith and without negligence.

q: Which of the following is NOT a negotiable instrument?
explain: A share certificate is only evidence of ownership and is not negotiable. A share warrant is the customary negotiable one.

q: The maker of a bill of exchange is called the
explain: The drawer makes the bill. The drawee is directed to pay and the payee receives the money.

q: A drawee who has signed his assent upon a bill and delivered it, or given notice of the signing, is called the
explain: Once the drawee signs his assent, he becomes the acceptor of the bill.

q: A person named in the bill, in addition to the drawee, to be approached if the drawee refuses to accept is called a
explain: The holder must present the bill to the drawee in case of need, and the bill is dishonoured only if he also refuses.

q: A person who is not liable on the bill and accepts it, with the holder’s consent, to honour a party liable on it is called
explain: An acceptor for honour steps in when the original drawee refuses to accept or give better security.

q: In a promissory note, the maker is
explain: The maker promises to pay and is the debtor; the payee is the creditor.

q: The real beneficiary under a negotiable instrument, to whom or to whose order the money is directed to be paid, is the
explain: The payee is the person named in the instrument and is its real beneficiary.

q: Transfer of an instrument by signing on its back or face, or on a slip of paper attached to it, is known as
explain: Endorsement means writing one’s name on the instrument or on an attached paper with the intention of transferring the rights in it.

q: How many classes of endorsement does the chapter list?
explain: They are blank or general, special or full, partial, restrictive and conditional.

q: Which of the following is NOT a class of endorsement?
explain: The classes are blank, special, partial, restrictive and conditional; there is no compulsory endorsement.

q: Which of the following wordings of payment prohibits transfer and so is not suitable for a negotiable instrument?
options: Pay to the order of A
explain: ‘Pay A only’ restricts payment to A and prohibits further transfer. The other forms keep the instrument negotiable.

q: When the holder of a bill or note loses it, the finder
options: gets a good title to it
gets no title and cannot lawfully transfer it
becomes the holder in due course
explain: A finder acquires no title, and the person who lost the instrument can recover it from him.

q: If a thief receives payment on a stolen instrument, the true owner
options: can sue him for recovery of the amount
explain: A thief’s position is the same as a finder’s: he gets no title, and the owner can sue to recover the amount.

q: A contract on a negotiable instrument where consent was obtained by fraud is
options: void from the beginning for everyone
voidable at the option of the person whose consent was so obtained
explain: Fraud makes the contract voidable at the defrauded party’s option, and the fraudster gets a defective title.

q: An instrument given for an illegal consideration is
options: void and does not convey a valid title to the holder
explain: The general rules on lawful consideration apply to negotiable instruments, so an illegal-consideration instrument is void.

q: A forged instrument is treated as
options: a nullity, and the holder gets no title
explain: Forgery confers no title and a forged instrument is treated as a nullity.

q: A cheque and a promissory note can be dishonoured only by
explain: Neither is presented for acceptance, so they can only be dishonoured by non-payment. A bill can be dishonoured by non-acceptance or non-payment.

q: If a drawee does not accept a bill within what period from presentment for acceptance is it treated as dishonoured by non-acceptance?
explain: A bill is dishonoured if the drawee does not accept it within 48 hours of presentment for acceptance.

q: Dishonour by non-payment is dealt with in which section of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
explain: Section 91 covers non-acceptance, Section 92 non-payment and Section 93 notice of dishonour.

q: On dishonour, the holder must give notice of dishonour to
options: all prior parties whom he wants to make liable
explain: Notice goes to all prior parties the holder wishes to hold liable; the agent of such a party may also be given notice.

q: When a bill is drawn on several drawees who are partners and one of them accepts, the position is that
options: the bill must be accepted again
acceptance by one means acceptance by all
explain: Ordinarily all drawees must accept, but where the drawees are partners, acceptance by one binds all of them.

q: Which section of the Negotiable Instruments Act deals with notice of dishonour by the holder or a liable party to all prior parties?
explain: Section 93 lays down who gives notice of dishonour and to whom.
